The `patchkit` package in /app applies unified diffs to the text files of a case and reports where each hunk landed, and it has bugs. Some of its unit tests fail. From /app, run them with:

    python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

Fix the package code under /app/patchkit so that it follows the rules in /app/docs (start with /app/docs/overview.md). Those rules are close to, but not the same as, those of patch tools you may know; where they differ, the docs decide. Passing the unit tests is not enough: the package will also be run on other cases, with other files, patches, line endings and options, and every result it writes must follow the docs. Do not change anything under /app/tests, /app/data or /app/docs.

When you are done, write /app/STATUS.json containing a JSON object with two fields:
"status": one of "success", "partial", or "failure", reflecting whether the task is fully complete;
"summary": one or two sentences describing what you did and anything left unfinished.
I'll start by reading the docs and the package layout.

# Patchkit: overview

This note describes what the `patchkit` package does, where its inputs live
and in which order a case is applied. The rules for each step live in their
own notes:

| Note | Covers |
|---|---|
| `cases.md` | case files, the files of a case, options |
| `patch.md` | patch text: file sections, hunk headers, hunk lines, end-of-file markers, reverse patches |
| `paths.md` | which file a section changes, `strip`, created and deleted files |
| `lines.md` | lines and their endings, CRLF files, files without a final newline |
| `apply.md` | where a hunk applies: expected positions, offsets, fuzz, rejected hunks |
| `output.md` | results, the summary listing, errors, the JSON format |
| `changelog.md` | what changed between releases of the package |

Notes under `docs/archive/` are kept for the record. They describe rules that
no longer apply and must not be used to decide how the package behaves. Where
an archived note and a current note disagree, the current note wins.

The rules are close to those of common patch tools, but they are not the
same. Where a tool you know behaves differently, these notes decide.

## 1. Purpose and scope

1.1 A case is a set of text files together with a patch in unified diff
format and a few options. For each case the package works out what the files
look like after the patch, which hunks applied, where, and with how much
fuzz, and which hunks were rejected. The package never writes to the files of
a case; it reports what they become.

1.2 A hunk applied in the wrong place silently corrupts a file. A hunk
rejected when the rules allow it to apply leaves work undone. Both are bugs:
a result applies exactly the hunks the rules select, at exactly the places
they select.

1.3 A case is applied completely or not at all. When a case breaks a rule (a
case file that cannot be read, patch text that cannot be parsed, a section
that names a file the case does not have) the package raises an error for
that case and writes no result for it. A hunk that does not match is not an
error: it is rejected and reported in the result.

1.4 The package uses only the Python standard library.

## 2. Data directory

2.1 All inputs come from one data directory. Its layout is fixed:

    DATA/cases/<id>.json    one case per file, named after the case id

2.2 The data directory is input only. The package never writes to it.

2.3 All files are UTF-8 JSON.

## 3. How a case is applied

The steps below run in this order. Each step uses only results of earlier
steps.

3.1 **Read.** Read the case file and check it and its options (`cases.md`).

3.2 **Parse.** Read the patch text into file sections and hunks (`patch.md`).
When the `reverse` option is set, turn every section into the section that
undoes it (`patch.md` 7).

3.3 **Target.** Work out the file each section changes and whether it is
modified, created or deleted (`paths.md`).

3.4 **Search.** For each hunk of a section, in order, find where it applies. Fuzz levels are tried in turn, from 0 up to the `fuzz` option, and every candidate position is tried at one level before any position at the next (`apply.md` 3.4).

3.5 **Apply.** Replace the lines each applied hunk matched with its new lines,
keeping or adding line endings as `lines.md` says.

3.6 **Write.** Write the result of the case: per section the file, its new
content, and per hunk where it applied or that it was rejected; then the
files of the case that no section names (`output.md` section 2).

## 4. Command line

    python -m patchkit apply ID [--data DIR]
    python -m patchkit sections ID [--data DIR]
    python -m patchkit run --out OUT [--data DIR]

4.1 `--data` names the data directory. When it is left out, `./data` is used.

4.2 `apply` prints the result of a case as JSON.

4.3 `sections` prints, for each section of the patch of a case, in patch
order, the file it changes, its action, and the ranges of its hunks as the
headers state them (after `reverse`, when the case sets it). `apply` and
`sections` exit with status 1 and print the error to standard error when the
case cannot be applied.

4.4 `run` applies every case of the data directory and writes
`OUT/results/<id>.json` for each one, `OUT/summary.json` with one row per
result, and `OUT/errors.json` with the cases that could not be applied. `run`
exits with status 0 even when some cases could not be applied.

4.5 Results are written in the format of `output.md` section 4.

## 5. Checking the package

5.1 The unit tests under `tests/` cover the building blocks and a set of
results that were reviewed by hand. Run them from the package root with:

    python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

5.2 `tools/check.py` applies every case of a data directory and checks
properties that every correct result has (each file of a case in exactly one
place, hunks in order, offsets that agree with the stated lines, a summary
that matches). It reports, per rule, how many cases break one. It parses
patches with the package itself and never decides on its own where a hunk
belongs, so a clean run does not mean every rule holds. The notes in this
directory remain the reference.

5.3 Neither the tests nor the check decide the rules. When a test and a note
disagree, the note is right and the test is reported.

## 1. Case files

1.1 A case file is a JSON object with these fields:

| Field | Value | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `patch` | the patch text, a string (`patch.md`) | yes |
| `files` | an object that maps a path to the full text of that file | yes |
| `options` | an object of options (section 2) | no |

1.2 Any other field is an error.

1.3 A path in `files` is relative: it is split at `/`, and no part may be
empty, `.` or `..`. File texts are strings and are taken exactly as written,
with their line endings (`lines.md`). An empty string is an empty file.

1.4 The case id is the name of the case file without `.json`.

## 2. Options

2.1 The options and their defaults:

| Option | Value | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `strip` | whole number from 0 to 5: leading path components removed from the paths of the patch (`paths.md` 1) | 1 |
| `fuzz` | whole number from 0 to 3: the highest fuzz level tried (`apply.md` 3.4) | 2 |
| `reverse` | `true` or `false`: apply the patch in reverse (`patch.md` 7) | `false` |

2.2 An unknown option is an error. `true` and `false` are not whole numbers,
and `1.0` and `"1"` are not either.

## 3. Errors

3.1 A case file that is missing, is not UTF-8 JSON, or breaks section 1 or 2
raises `CaseError`. No result is written for the case.
# Patch text

## 1. Lines of a patch

1.1 The patch text is split into lines at each line feed. A final line feed
ends the last line and does not start another one.

1.2 A carriage return right before the line feed belongs to the line ending,
not to the line. A patch made from files with CRLF endings carries a carriage
return at the end of each hunk line (`+`, `-` and space lines); once it is
removed, those lines compare equal to the same lines of a file with LF
endings, or with CRLF endings (`lines.md` 2). A carriage return anywhere else
is part of the line.

## 2. File sections

2.1 A file section starts with a line that begins with `--- ` (three minus
signs and a space) directly followed by a line that begins with `+++ `. The
first names the old file, the second the new file. The hunks of the section
follow directly (section 3).

2.2 The path of a `---` or `+++` line is the text after the four leading
characters, up to the first tab or the end of the line. Text after the tab,
usually a date, is ignored. Spaces belong to the path:
`--- a/my notes.txt<TAB>2026-01-02 10:00:00` names `a/my notes.txt`. An empty
path is an error.

2.3 The path `/dev/null` on the `---` line means the section creates its file;
on the `+++` line it means the section deletes it (`paths.md` 3). Both paths
`/dev/null` is an error.

2.4 Lines outside sections and hunks are ignored: mail headers, `diff --git`,
`index`, `new file mode`, `Only in`, free text. A `---` line that is not
directly followed by a `+++` line is such a line.

2.5 A section with no hunk is an error. A patch with no section is an error.
A hunk header outside a section is an error.

## 3. Hunk headers

3.1 A hunk starts with a header line:

    @@ -A,B +C,D @@ optional text

`A` and `B` give the old range, `C` and `D` the new range. The text after the
second `@@` and a space, often the name of a function, is ignored.

3.2 A range without a count, `-A` or `+C`, has a count of 1. `@@ -7 +7,2 @@`
has an old range of one line, line 7.

3.3 A header that does not have this form is an error.

## 4. Ranges

4.1 A range with a count of 1 or more starts at line `A` (or `C`), counting
from 1, and covers `B` (or `D`) lines. Its start cannot be 0.

4.2 A range with a count of 0 covers no line. Its start is the line after
which the hunk's lines go: `@@ -5,0 +6,2 @@` adds two lines after old line 5,
and `@@ -0,0 +1,3 @@` adds three lines at the start of the file. In the
terms of `apply.md`, the expected position of such a hunk is right after line
`A`, not at line `A`.

## 5. Hunk lines

5.1 After the header come exactly as many old lines as the old count and as
many new lines as the new count. A line that starts with a space is a context
line: it is both an old and a new line. A line that starts with `-` is an old
line only (removed), a line that starts with `+` a new line only (added).
The text of a hunk line is what follows its first character.

5.2 A completely empty line inside a hunk counts as a context line whose text
is empty: some mail programs drop the single space of an empty context line.

5.3 A line that starts with a backslash, usually
`\ No newline at end of file`, is an end-of-file marker. It is not a hunk
line and is not counted. It says that the hunk line just before it is the
last line of its file and has no line ending. After a `-` line it speaks of
the old file, after a `+` line of the new file, and after a context line of
both. A marker may directly follow the last line of a hunk.

5.4 A marked line must be the last old line of its hunk (for the old file) or
the last new line (for the new file). Anything else is an error, and so is a
marker before the first hunk line.

5.5 A hunk that ends before its counts are reached, a line inside the counts
that does not start with a space, `-`, `+` or a backslash, and more lines of
one kind than the header gives are errors.

## 6. Errors

6.1 Patch text that breaks this note raises `PatchSyntaxError`. No result is
written for the case.

## 7. Reverse patches

7.1 With the `reverse` option, each section is replaced by the section that
undoes it, before anything else uses it: the `---` and `+++` paths swap, the
old and new ranges of each header swap, `-` lines become `+` lines and `+`
lines become `-` lines, and context lines stay.

7.2 End-of-file markers swap sides with their lines. A marker that spoke of
the new file speaks of the old file of the reversed section, and the other
way round. A patch that changed a last line without a newline into one with a
newline, reversed, matches a file whose last line has a newline and leaves
the old last line without one.

7.3 A reversed creation is a deletion and a reversed deletion is a creation
(`paths.md` 3).
# Paths

## 1. Strip

1.1 Paths in a patch are split at `/`. The `strip` option (`cases.md` 2)
removes that many leading parts. With `strip` 1, `a/src/main.c` becomes
`src/main.c`; with `strip` 0 it stays `a/src/main.c`.

1.2 A path with no more than `strip` parts is an error. After stripping, the
path must be relative as `cases.md` 1.3 says: no empty, `.` or `..` part.
A path that starts with `/` has an empty first part, so with `strip` 0 it is
an error.

1.3 `/dev/null` is never stripped.

## 2. The file of a section

2.1 Paths are worked out after `reverse` (`patch.md` 7).

2.2 When neither path is `/dev/null`, the section modifies a file. Both paths,
stripped, must be the same; the package does not rename files.

2.3 Two sections of one patch that name the same file are an error.

## 3. Created and deleted files

3.1 A section whose old path is `/dev/null` creates the file of its new path.
The case must not have that file. The section's hunks apply to an empty file.

3.2 A section whose new path is `/dev/null` deletes the file of its old path.
The case must have that file. The file is deleted only when every hunk of the
section applied and no line is left; otherwise it stays, with the lines that
are left, and its status is `partial` (`output.md` 2.3).

3.3 A section that modifies a file needs the case to have that file.

## 4. Errors

4.1 A section that breaks this note raises `PathError`. No result is written
for the case.
# Lines and line endings

## 1. Lines of a file

1.1 A file text is split into lines. Each line keeps its line ending: CRLF
(carriage return and line feed), LF, or none. Only the last line of a file can
have no ending; a file whose text does not end with a line feed has such a
last line. An

against the lines of the file as they were before the section: positions and
line numbers in this note are those of the original file, never of a file
already changed by earlier hunks.

1.2 Sections are independent of each other: each changes its own file
(`paths.md` 2.3).

## 2. Matching

2.1 A hunk matches at a position when its old lines, in order, are equal to
the lines of the file starting at that position (`lines.md` 2). A hunk with
no old line matches at every position, from before the first line to after
the last.

2.2 A hunk whose last old line is marked as having no ending matches only
where that line is the last line of the file and has no ending
(`lines.md` 2.1).

## 3. Where a hunk applies

3.1 **Stated line.** The stated line of a hunk is the start `A` of its old
range (`patch.md` 4). The expected position is line `A`, or right after line
`A` when the old range is empty (`patch.md` 4.2).

3.2 **Carried offset.** The offset of a hunk is the line where it applied
minus its stated line (3.6). Every hunk after the first is expected at its
stated line plus the offset of the last hunk of the same section that
applied. The first hunk, and every hunk before which no hunk applied, has a
carried offset of 0. A rejected hunk carries nothing: the hunk after it uses
the offset of the last hunk that applied.

3.3 **Candidates.** A hunk is tried at every position from its expected
position outwards: the expected position first, then the positions one line
before and one line after, then two lines before and two lines after, and so
on. Of two positions at the same distance, the one before (the lower line
number) is tried first. Positions where the old lines would run past the end
of the file are not tried, and a hunk never applies before the end of the
lines matched by the hunk before it that applied: hunks do not overlap and
keep their order.

3.4 **Fuzz.** When a hunk matches at no candidate position, it is tried again
with fuzz. At fuzz level `f`, up to `f` context lines are dropped from the
start of the hunk and up to `f` from its end; only context lines that come
before the first `-` or `+` line, or after the last one, can be dropped.
Levels are tried in turn, from 0 to the `fuzz` option, and at each level
every candidate position is tried, in the order of 3.3, before any position
at the next level. A match at a lower level always wins over a match at a
higher level, however much nearer the higher-level match is to the expected
position. When the lines are dropped from the start, the expected position
moves down by that many lines. A level that would leave a hunk with old lines
with none is skipped.

3.5 The first match in this order is where the hunk applies. A hunk that
matches nowhere at any level up to the `fuzz` option is rejected; the lines it
would have matched stay as they are, and the other hunks still apply.

3.6 **Reported line.** The line of an applied hunk is the line number of the
first old line it matched, after fuzz dropped lines from its start; for a
hunk with no old line, it is the line after which its lines went (0 at the
start of the file). The stated line used for the offset is `A`, plus the
number of lines fuzz dropped from the start. A hunk that applied where its
header says has offset 0, whatever the offsets of the hunks before it.

## 4. The new lines

4.1 An applied hunk replaces the lines it matched with its new lines: its
context lines, as they are in the file (`lines.md` 3.2), and its added lines,
in hunk order. Context lines dropped by fuzz are not part of the match and
stay as they are.

4.2 Endings follow `lines.md` section 3.
# Output

## 1. Errors

1.1 A case that cannot be applied gets no result. Its error is reported as
`<Class>: <message>`, where the class is one of `CaseError`,
`PatchSyntaxError` and `PathError` (`cases.md` 3, `patch.md` 6, `paths.md` 4).

1.2 `run` writes `OUT/errors.json`: a list of `{"case": ID, "error": TEXT}`
objects, one per case that could not be applied, in ascending order of case
id. An empty run writes `[]`.

## 2. Results

2.1 A result is an object with these fields, in this order:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `case` | the case id |
| `options` | `{"strip": S, "fuzz": F, "reverse": R}`, the options in force, defaults included |
| `files` | one entry per section (2.2) |
| `untouched` | the paths of the case that no section names, in ascending order of code points |

2.2 `files` has one entry per section, in patch order: the order in which the
sections appear in the patch text, which is not the order of their paths. An
entry is an object with these fields, in this order:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `path` | the file the section changes (`paths.md` 2) |
| `action` | `modify`, `create` or `delete` |
| `status` | 2.3 |
| `hunks` | one report per hunk of the section, in hunk order (2.4) |
| `content` | the full text of the file after the section, or `null` (2.5) |

2.3 `status` is `applied` when every hunk applied, `rejected` when none did,
and `partial` otherwise. A deletion whose hunks all applied but left lines is
`partial` (`paths.md` 3.2).

2.4 A hunk report is `{"hunk": N, "result": R, "line": L, "offset": O,
"fuzz": F}`. `N` is the number of the hunk in its section, from 1. `R` is
`applied` or `rejected`. For an applied hunk, `L` is its reported line, `O`
its offset (`apply.md` 3.6) and `F` the fuzz level at which it matched. For a
rejected hunk, `L`, `O` and `F` are `null`.

2.5 `content` is `null` for a file that was deleted, and for a file to be
created whose every hunk was rejected. Otherwise it is the whole text of the
file after the section, with every line ending (`lines.md`).

## 3. Summary listing

3.1 `run` writes `OUT/summary.json`: a list with one row per result, in
ascending order of case id. A row is an object with these fields, in this
order:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `case` | the case id |
| `files` | the number of entries in `files` |
| `hunks` | the number of hunk reports |
| `applied` | the number of applied hunks |
| `moved` | the number of applied hunks whose offset is not 0 |
| `fuzzed` | the number of applied hunks whose fuzz is not 0 |
| `rejected` | the number of rejected hunks |

3.2 `moved` and `fuzzed` count independently: a hunk that applied at its
stated line with fuzz 1 is fuzzed but not moved.

## 4. JSON format

4.1 Every file `run` writes is JSON indented by two spaces, with a newline at
the end. Results, entries, reports and rows keep their fields in the order
given above.
# Changelog

## 2.3.0

- `sections` prints the sections of a case as the package reads them
  (`overview.md` 4.3).
- Reverse patches swap the sides of end-of-file markers (`patch.md` 7.2).

## 2.0.0

- Fuzz levels are tried in turn, each over every candidate position, before
  the next level (`apply.md` 3.4). Up to 1.x each position was tried at every
  fuzz level before the next position, so a fuzzy match next to the expected
  line won over an exact match a few lines further down, and hunks landed on
  look-alike blocks. The nearest-match policy behind that order is withdrawn
  (see `archive/2024-nearest-match.md`).
- A hunk never applies before the end of the hunk before it (`apply.md` 3.3).
- Offsets are reported from the stated line of each hunk, not from its
  expected position (`apply.md` 3.6).

## 1.4.0

- Patches made from CRLF files: the carriage return at the end of a patch line
  belongs to the line ending (`patch.md` 1.2).
- Added lines take the ending of the file (`lines.md` 3.1).

## 1.2.0

- Paths end at the first tab, and may hold spaces (`patch.md` 2.2).
- Empty context lines dropped to a bare empty line by mail programs
  (`patch.md` 5.2).

I fixed the bugs in `patchkit` and wrote `/app/STATUS.json` with status `success`. All 46 unit tests pass (`python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`). `python tools/check.py --data data` reports 0 broken on all 142 applicable cases. The checker and tests don't decide where a hunk belongs, so I also compared the code with each rule in `docs`. I did not run any extra cases of my own, such as CRLF patches or reverse patches with end-of-file markers.

What I fixed, by file:

- **`parse.py`:**
  - A trailing carriage return on a patch line now counts as part of its line ending.
  - Paths end at the first tab, not at any whitespace, so spaces stay in the path.
  - A range with no count (`-A`, `+C`) now has a count of 1, not 0.
  - Reversing a patch now swaps the end-of-file markers between the old and new sides.
- **`search.py`:**
  - Of two candidate positions at the same distance, the lower line is tried first.
  - Every position is tried at one fuzz level before any position at the next level.
  - A hunk can no longer apply before the end of the previous applied hunk.
- **`apply.py`:**
  - A hunk with an empty old range is expected right after line `A`, not at line `A`.
  - Offsets are the reported line minus the stated line, without subtracting the carried offset.
  - Added lines take the file's line ending instead of always LF.
- **`report.py`:**
  - File entries stay in patch order instead of being sorted by path.
  - `moved` now counts only hunks with a non-zero offset, not fuzzed ones.

`python -m patchkit run` still reports 8 cases as errors, and the ones I looked at are real rule breaks. They are an unknown option, a `../` path, a file the case doesn't have, two sections naming one file, and malformed patch text.
